catalog_quote: 2.3 Tones in Baba I This section is aimed at acquainting the reader with the tone patterns and possible tonal phenomena attested in Baba I which is a tone language. Steven Bird (1999d) considers a tone language as one in which voice pitch on an individual syllable may carry either a lexically or grammatically contrastive meaning. Welmers (1959: 2) sees a tone language as one in which both pitch phonemes and segmental phonemes enter into the composition of at least some morphemes. This means that some morphemes may lack a pitch phoneme while others may be exclusively made up of a tone without any segmental components or tone bearing units. It is in line with the above view that our analysis of Baba I tonal system is based. ... In Baba I there are principally two basic or underlying tones; high and low which manifest themselves on the surface in varying patterns and levels depending on the nature of the morpheme or segment over which they have domain and the environment in which they occur. 2.3.1 Level tones These are single tonemes assigned to single tone bearing units in well defined contexts.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Baba 1 is described as a tone language with two underlying level tones (H, L) on each tone-bearing unit, plus derived contour tones, downstep and floating tones; the only full description of the language says nothing about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal detail only (contour tones limited to two tonemes per TBU and mostly phrase-derived; toneless grammatical morphemes acquire tone by spreading).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on morphemes/words in citation form; tone rules (docking, spreading, downstep) apply across word boundaries in associative and verb constructions. No stress domain stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Baba 1 (su papiax 'speech of the Baba 1 people'; Papia/Bapa/Bapakum, Ethnologue bbw), Ndop plain, Ngoketunjia Division, NW Cameroon = Glottolog baba1264; author is a native speaker. Explicitly distinct from Baba 2 (a Ngemba variety in Mezam Division).

new_statements.quote: p.52: "This section is aimed at acquainting the reader with the tone patterns and possible tonal phenomena attested in Baba I which is a tone language." p.53: "In Baba I there are principally two basic or underlying tones; high and low which manifest themselves on the surface in varying patterns and levels depending on the nature of the morpheme or segment over which they have domain and the environment in which they occur." p.64: "Baba 1 is a four-tone language with two level tones (low and high) and two contour tones (rising and falling). The level tones are the basic tonemes in this language and the contour tones occur as a result of connected speech or compounding." p.148: "A cleft sentence is therefore a type of focus construction and it is used as a normal device for focusing mostly in languages where focus is not marked by prosodic prominence. This is exactly the type of form Baba 1 employs in order to bring into focus its argument structures."

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same work the existing statement was taken from; the pp.52-53 quotation is confirmed verbatim against the page scan. The catalog record for Baba 1 has an empty rule; this source supports keeping it as a tone language with no stress statement rather than any stress placement. Adds the p.64 four-tone (two level, two contour) description and the p.148 remark that focus is not marked by prosodic prominence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The work describes Baba 1 as a tone language with two underlying tones (H, L), surface rising and falling contours arising in connected speech or compounding, downstep, floating tones and leftward tone docking; syllable peaks are vowels and tone-bearing nasals; vowel length is phonemic (p.21). The words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur in reference to Baba 1 (the single 'pitch accent' hit, p.3, is a remark about the scope of autosegmental theory). The only prominence remark is phrase-level: the author says focus is not marked by prosodic prominence but by clefting (p.148).
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement to have exceptions)
new_statements.identity_note: Nashipu 2005 describes Baba 1 (Papia/Bapakum), the Nun-group Grassfields Bantu language of the Baba 1 village in the Ndop plain, Northwest Region, Cameroon; no dialect is singled out. It is not Baba (the Bamileke/Ngiemboon-area variety) or Baba 2.
